passage: Mohit lined up the medals in his head: cricket for Rehan, drawing for Tia, chess for Kabir. And him? Nothing. He said it out loud in the lift to Sudha Aunty from the third floor. "I'm not special at anything." She pressed the button for the ground floor. "You're ten, Mohit. Nobody is finished at ten. Come to my Saturday club and just try things." On Saturday his clay bowl leaned like a tired tower. He laughed, hands full of grey clay, and Sudha Aunty laughed too. Later he tried the drum, badly, and loved the noise. In the lift on the way home he was thinking about next Saturday, not about medals.

qa.q: Where did Mohit tell Sudha Aunty that he was not special at anything?
qa.a: He said it in the lift.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he lined up his friends' medals and found nothing for himself?
qa.a: He felt insecure and ordinary, as if everyone else had something and he had nothing.
Going to Sudha Aunty's Saturday club and trying different things, enjoying them without needing to be the best.

qa.q: How might Sudha Aunty see Mohit's worry?
qa.a: As common at his age. She sees a child still early in finding what he likes, so she invites him to try things instead of compete.

grounding: Shows a child certain he has no special talent who finds enjoyment in trying different things.

passage:
I'm Ritu. Last year it felt like everyone in my class had a thing. Gurleen dances. Arun does maths in his head. Tina draws horses. I had nothing. When the teacher asked us to write "My special talent", I wrote "I don't know" and then rubbed it out, because it looked sad.
Then Mummy said, "Nobody your age knows their talent yet. Try things." So I did. Chess club: I lost every game. Choir: I was okay. Then pottery at the summer camp. My first pot collapsed. So did the second. But I loved the cold, wet clay, and I forgot the time.
I'm still not the best at anything. But now when someone asks, I say, "I'm trying pottery," and that feels good.

qa.q: What happened to Ritu's first pot?
How did Ritu feel when asked to write a special talent?
qa.a: Insecure and sad, believing Ritu had nothing special at all.

qa.q: What advice helped Ritu, and what came of it?
qa.a: Mummy's advice to try things; Ritu found pottery enjoyable even without being the best at it.

qa.q: What would change if Ritu only valued being the best?
qa.a: Ritu might have quit pottery after the collapsed pots and missed the joy of the cold, wet clay.

grounding: A child who believes they are good at nothing special tries different activities and finds that enjoying them matters more than being the best.

passage:
Summer camp counsellor's note, Day 5
On Monday, when we went round the circle naming something we're good at, Seema whispered, "Nothing," and hid her face in her knees. The others said dancing, cricket, drawing.
I told her that talents often take years to show up, and asked her to try one new thing each day this week. Tuesday, clay: she laughed at her wonky bowl. Wednesday, cricket: bored. Thursday, the nature trail with Ayesha: she found three kinds of beetles and named them all.
Today she ran to me holding a leaf with a caterpillar on it. "Can I be in charge of the bug box?" I said yes. She didn't ask whether she was the best at it. She just looked happy. I will tell her parents about the beetles.

qa.q: How many kinds of beetles did Seema find?
What did Seema's "Nothing" and hidden face suggest on Monday?
qa.a: She felt insecure and embarrassed, believing she had no talent.

qa.q: What did the camp counsellor suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Trying one new thing each day, which let Seema discover she loves insects without needing to be the best.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have seen Seema on the nature trail?
qa.a: As a keen trail partner, excitedly spotting and naming beetles.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a girl who thinks she is good at nothing trying different things and finding joy in one of them.
